SASRec already learns adaptive recency weighting: its original study finds stronger attention to recent actions on sparse Amazon data and broader historical attention on dense MovieLens. It truncates inputs to the latest n interactions; sequence-length experiments show that longer histories help on MovieLens, so aggressive truncation is a control to test, not an assumed improvement. [SASRec](https://arxiv.org/html/1808.09781)

Established alternatives support separating simple aggregation from learned selection. HGN combines feature gating, instance gating, and explicit item–item interactions; its ablations include average/max pooling and removing individual components. These establish useful controls but do not directly demonstrate that adding an adaptive long/short fusion gate to SASRec beats tuned fixed fusion. LS4SRec also uses the average embedding of the latest k items as a short-term supervision target, supporting recent-item averaging as a reasonable baseline rather than proving its standalone ranking performance. [HGN](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.09217), [LS4SRec](https://doi.org/10.1145/3723173)

Recommended experiment, inferred from these findings: compare unchanged SASRec; SASRec trained with shorter recent-history windows; recent-k embedding averages alone; fixed fusion h = (1−α)h_SASRec + α mean(e_recent); a learned global scalar α; and a history-conditioned gate using identical branches. Tune k and α on validation, exclude padding from averages, and keep training budgets and candidate sets comparable. Adaptive gating adds evidence of value only if it improves the four-category macro validation HR@10 beyond the best truncation and fixed-fusion controls; report category results to expose uneven gains. Existing papers do not establish that outcome for this pinned RecHarness setting.
